feedback: If the line does not cross PQ at its midpoint, check whether the two sets of arcs have equal radii: unequal radii make a KITE (the line is perpendicular to PQ but does not bisect it), equal radii make a rhombus (the line is perpendicular to PQ AND bisects it).

If equal-radius arcs do not cross at two points, check the opening: below half PQ they do not meet; at exactly half they touch only at the midpoint. Use an opening greater than half PQ and allow enough space on the page.

If there are no arcs on the page and the midpoint was found with a ruler or the angle judged by eye, that is drawing, not constructing: redo it so every point of the line is equidistant from P and Q, shown by equal arcs.
Keeping the compass width unchanged between P and Q is the whole point — it is what forces the rhombus.
activities.intendedInsight: Every point on the perpendicular bisector is equidistant from P and Q. Equal-radius arcs locate two such points, and the straight line through them is the perpendicular bisector; visible arcs make the method inspectable, though arcs alone do not prove they were placed correctly.
learnerActions: Take a line segment PQ drawn diagonally (not horizontal or vertical), a pair of compasses and a straight edge — no ruler measuring and no protractor.
Open the compasses to MORE than half of PQ; discuss why an opening of half or less means the arcs only touch or never meet, and why an enormous opening just wastes space.
Place the compass point on P and sweep an arc above and below the segment; WITHOUT changing the radius, place the point on Q and sweep again so the arcs cross at two points.
Rule the straight line through the two crossing points, leaving all construction arcs visible as evidence of method.
Explain why the line passes through the midpoint at 90°: the four equal radii form a rhombus, whose diagonals perpendicularly bisect each other.
Repeat on segments at several different orientations, not only horizontal/vertical ones.
activities.title: Construct the perpendicular bisector with compasses and straight edge

feedback: If the line does not appear to split the angle equally, check that the two inner arcs were drawn with the same radius from each arm-crossing point.

Leave your arcs visible — they show you constructed the bisector from equal lengths rather than measuring halves with a protractor. (The congruent halves follow from the equal arcs, so no measuring is needed to justify it.)
activities.intendedInsight: The same equidistance principle that bisects a segment also bisects an angle — one property, reused, rather than a second memorised routine.
learnerActions: Take a marked angle (try one at a non-standard orientation), compasses and a straight edge.
Place the compass point at the vertex and sweep an arc that crosses both arms of the angle at two points.
WITHOUT changing the radius, place the point on each of those two crossing points in turn and sweep equal arcs that meet inside the angle.
Rule the line from the vertex through that meeting point, leaving the arcs visible.
Explain how this reuses the equal-radius property: equal lengths from the vertex and equal arcs from the arm-crossings force the two halves to be congruent, so the line bisects the angle.
activities.title: Bisect an angle using the same equal-arc idea

feedback: If the circle centred at A only touches l or misses it, increase the radius until it meets l twice. A single touch does not provide distinct B and C for this construction.
If an arc crossing coincides with A, use the other crossing, or adjust the common radius so D is distinct from A; two distinct points are needed to draw AD.
If the perpendicular does not pass through A, return to the given point and the equidistance argument. A perpendicular somewhere else on the line does not meet this task.
activities.intendedInsight: A point equidistant from B and C lies on their perpendicular bisector. Finding a second distinct equidistant point locates a perpendicular through the given off-line point without measuring a right angle.
learnerActions: Draw a line l and a point A not on it. With centre A, choose a compass radius large enough for a circle to cross l at two distinct points B and C; extend l with the straight edge if needed.
Using equal radii from B and C, each greater than half BC, draw crossing arcs to locate a point D off l and distinct from A. Draw the straight line through A and D, keeping the arcs visible.
Explain why AB = AC and DB = DC place both A and D on the perpendicular bisector of BC. Since B and C lie on l, AD is perpendicular to l. Mark the foot H where AD meets l.
Explain that AH is the shortest distance from A to l. Repeat with a rotated line and A on the other side.
activities.title: Construct a perpendicular from a point off a line

feedback: If B and C are not equally far from A, redraw them using the same circle centred at A; estimating their positions by eye does not establish that A is the midpoint.
If the arcs from B and C fail to cross away from l, increase their common radius beyond half BC.
A measured 90° angle can be an accuracy check, but explain the equal distances to justify why the construction works.
activities.intendedInsight: The given point on the line can be made the midpoint of a constructed segment BC, so its perpendicular bisector passes through that point.
learnerActions: Draw a line l with a given point A on it. Draw a circle centred at A to mark B and C on l, on opposite sides of A, so AB = AC.
Without changing the compass opening between B and C, draw equal-radius arcs from them, using a radius greater than half BC, to meet at D off l.
Rule AD and leave the arcs visible. Explain that A is the midpoint of BC and both A and D are equidistant from B and C, so AD is the perpendicular bisector of BC and is perpendicular to l at A.

Try a sloping line and then explain how this task differs from constructing a perpendicular through a point off the line. After the construction, a protractor can check practical accuracy without replacing the property-based justification.
activities.title: Construct a perpendicular at a point on a line
